title: Where Did the “Social Magic” Go? - Nautilus
gist: Icelandic sociologist Vidar Halldorsson argues the digital age is a paradox: we are more globally connected yet less able to bond, because screens strip out 'social magic' — the micro-expressions, body language, proximity and even smell exchanged in shared physical space that build society.

insights.claim: Icelandic sociologist Vidar Halldorsson argues that although humans are more connected and accessible globally and immediately, our ability to bond using all the senses is eroding, leaving us less connected overall.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Supports secular demand for in-person experiences and skepticism of purely digital social products.
insights.quote: With our handheld supercomputers at the ready, we are less connected to one another in the end, not more.
insights.locator: Our digital age presents a paradox

insights.claim: Halldorsson coins 'social magic' for the tiny signals and exchanges of energy and empathy that arise from sharing physical space with another person and help build a society.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: A lens on what remote/digital interaction loses — relevant to the remote-work and social-media debates.
insights.locator: This is not a new idea

insights.claim: Facial micro-expressions, body language, spatial proximity and even smell all carry social information, according to Halldorsson.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Identifies channels that video and text platforms fail to transmit.
insights.locator: This is not a new idea

insights.claim: Halldorsson's social magic parallels what Émile Durkheim might have called 'collective effervescence', the sense of being part of something larger than oneself.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Ties modern loneliness concerns to classical sociology of shared rituals and gatherings.
insights.locator: This is not a new idea
